text: **S11 · Biological observation candidate · Infrared spectroscopy**

pages.title: S11 Infrared absorption spectroscopy
text: **S11 · Biological observation candidate · Infrared spectroscopy**

Infrared absorption spectroscopy measures wavelength-dependent attenuation associated with molecular vibrations. A spectrum can reveal chemical composition and changes in a sample, but the optical path and measurement format strongly influence the signal. Water and substrate contributions can dominate biologically interesting features.
## Signal and useful question

The output is absorbance or transmittance against wavenumber, commonly in inverse centimetres. Candidate questions concern whether a reproducible chemical pattern can be measured in a permitted sample format and whether it relates to a defined research phenotype. It should not be assumed that an ordinary closed culture plate offers a suitable infrared transmission path.
## Keep assay format explicit

Transmission, reflection and attenuated-total-reflection arrangements do not produce interchangeable observations. A contact measurement can require a different handling workflow from non-contact plate imaging. The product description should identify that difference before discussing automation or throughput.

Infrared spectroscopy is an exploratory candidate across the broader platform. The proposed qualification should compare repeated observations of reference materials and then assess the chosen biological question with appropriate controls. A classifier’s apparent accuracy should be challenged for dependence on medium, preparation batch or instrument background. No clinical identity or susceptibility function is established by including this modality in the catalogue.
tables: Wavenumber accuracy, background spectrum, optical path and instrument response.
Water absorption, vessel material, sample thickness, contact pressure and baseline correction.
Suitable infrared optics and detector; potentially a separate sample interface or preparation route.
Stable spectral information that survives realistic sample and instrument variation.

pages.title: S12 Optical coherence tomography
text: **S12 · Biological observation candidate · Depth-resolved optical research**

Optical coherence tomography uses interferometric information to resolve optical path differences within a sample. It can produce depth profiles and cross-sectional representations of scattering structures. The relationship between optical path length and physical depth depends on refractive properties and the reconstruction model. [R57]
## Signal and useful question

Candidate outputs include depth-dependent backscatter and reconstructed structural coordinates, with depth expressed in micrometres or millimetres under declared assumptions. Research questions could concern surface structure, thickness or subsurface morphology that a two-dimensional plate image cannot resolve.
## Distinguish structure from biological meaning

A reconstructed surface is a model-dependent measurement, not a direct resistance result. Features may arise from the medium or vessel rather than the growth being studied. The observation should therefore remain linked to a conventional overview and to the region selected for depth imaging.

This modality is a future research option, not a requirement for endpoint Reader V1. A development study should begin with known structural references and evaluate how vessel and medium effects alter reconstruction. Only then should it assess the intended biological application and the additional value relative to simpler focus, stereo or surface-imaging methods.
tables: Axial and lateral scales, reference surfaces, sensitivity range and reconstruction settings.
Multiple scattering, refractive-index variation, vessel reflections, shadowing and motion.
Interferometric optics, scanning or specialized detection, stable alignment and substantial data processing.
Depth information that is accurate enough and relevant enough to justify the added system complexity.

pages.title: S13 Quantitative phase imaging
text: **S13 · Biological observation candidate · Quantitative optical phase**

Quantitative phase imaging estimates changes in the phase of transmitted light caused by optical path differences. For a suitable sample, the signal relates to both thickness and refractive-index variation. Separating those contributions or converting them into another biological quantity requires additional assumptions and calibration.
## Signal and useful question

The primary output is phase in radians or optical path difference in length units. Candidate research questions include cell or microcolony growth, morphology and temporal changes that produce weak intensity contrast. Dry-mass estimates, where scientifically justified, are derived quantities rather than direct balance measurements.
## Respect the sample geometry

A method suitable for thin cells in a controlled optical path may not transfer to a thick, scattering agar plate. The proposed platform should treat cell-level phase research as a separate acquisition route with its own sample and field-selection records.

The evaluation should distinguish numerical reconstruction error from uncertainty in the biological interpretation. A phase map may be repeatable while an inferred mass is biased by an incorrect refractive increment. This candidate should be selected only where its assumptions can be tested and where the resulting measurement answers a question that ordinary intensity imaging cannot address adequately.
tables: Phase or path-length reference, background correction, spatial scale and reconstruction verification.
Phase wrapping, multiple scattering, refractive-index changes, drift and overlapping structures.
Interferometric or computational phase optics, stable illumination and a suitable thin-sample geometry.
Reproducible phase information with a defensible link to the intended research quantity.

pages.title: S14 Laser speckle activity sensing
text: **S14 · Biological observation candidate · Dynamic scattering research**

Laser speckle imaging records interference patterns produced when coherent light is scattered. Temporal changes in those patterns can reflect movement or other changes in the scattering scene. They can also arise from vibration, source instability or optical-path changes unrelated to biology.
## Signal and useful question

Candidate outputs include speckle contrast, correlation decay and other dimensionless temporal descriptors. Published plate-related studies have investigated speckle observations for early antibacterial-effect research. These are method-specific precedents, not established AMReye.AI performance. [R42] [R43]
## Compare against an instrument-only explanation

An early change in a speckle statistic should be challenged with controls that can reveal non-biological motion. The analysis should also preserve the relationship between exposure duration, sampling interval and the reported temporal feature.

This is an exploratory sensing pathway. Its first product contribution might be an additional research observation rather than an early clinical category. Any future susceptibility inference would need a defined clock origin, organism and drug scope, comparator and treatment of unreadable or inconsistent cases. A shorter detection window in an external study cannot be transferred to a different optical assembly by analogy alone.
tables: Stable scattering references, exposure timing, optical alignment and instrument-motion characterization.
Vibration, evaporation, thermal drift, motion of the vessel and changes in illumination coherence.
Coherent source, optical containment, mechanically stable acquisition and time-series analysis.
A biological signal that remains distinguishable from instrument and environmental dynamics.

pages.title: S15 Elastic light scattering
text: **S15 · Biological observation candidate · Angular scattering**

Elastic light scattering measures light redirected by an object without a change in photon frequency. The angular and intensity distribution depends on size, shape, refractive properties and the measurement geometry. In a heterogeneous biological sample, several structures can contribute to the same pattern.
## Signal and useful question

The instrument may record intensity against angle or a two-dimensional scattering pattern. Normalized descriptors are generally dimensionless; absolute intensity requires a calibrated optical response. Candidate questions concern whether a stable pattern can characterize a sample or flag a change that deserves further observation.
## Avoid one-to-one biological assumptions

A scattering pattern is not uniquely determined by organism identity or susceptibility. Different combinations of shape, concentration and refractive properties can produce similar observations. A learned classifier may exploit stable laboratory artifacts rather than the desired biological variation.

The proposed evaluation should include repeated measurements after repositioning and across permitted sample containers. Where a biological inference is investigated, it should be compared with a suitable reference and tested outside the acquisition batches used for development. The initial role is research characterization; a direct clinical conclusion would require substantially more evidence than pattern separation on a small dataset.
tables: Angular geometry, source stability, detector response and reference scattering objects.
Vessel curvature, multiple scattering, sample concentration, alignment and stray reflections.
Controlled source-detector geometry, baffling and a reproducible sample presentation.
Pattern stability and useful discrimination after vessel and concentration effects are controlled.

pages.title: S16 Nephelometric turbidity sensing
text: **S16 · Preparation quality candidate · Nephelometric measurement**

Nephelometry measures light scattered by suspended material at a defined observation geometry. It can support a turbidity comparison used in inoculum preparation workflows. Its output depends on particle properties and instrument geometry, so it should not be treated as a universal cell counter.
## Signal and useful question

The output may be an instrument response, a calibrated turbidity unit or a comparison with an applicable McFarland reference. The useful question is whether the preparation falls within the method’s permitted turbidity condition. A McFarland value and a viable count in CFU per millilitre are not interchangeable measurements.
## Keep preparation QC distinct from final AST

A preparation check can reduce one source of assay variation, but it does not establish that the rest of the assay was performed correctly. The record should retain the turbidity observation, its reference basis and any action taken, rather than storing only a generic “QC passed” flag.

An integrated nephelometric pathway is a proposed module. It should be evaluated independently and then as part of the selected laboratory workflow. If an organism or sample type produces an atypical optical relationship, the system should preserve the limitation rather than convert the response into an unsupported precise viable-cell concentration. [R03]
tables: Appropriate turbidity references, vessel path, detector response and repeatability checks.
Cell size, clumping, non-cell particles, bubbles, tube scratches and settling.
Defined sample holder, optical geometry, cleanable surfaces and preparation-record linkage.
Reliable method-relevant comparison across the permitted sample and vessel range.

pages.title: S17 Absorbance and optical density
text: **S17 · Biological observation candidate · Optical attenuation**

Absorbance-related measurements compare incident and transmitted light. A common expression is A = −log10(I/I0), where I is the sample signal and I0 is an appropriate reference. In microbial suspensions, scattering can contribute strongly, so an optical-density reading is not necessarily a pure molecular absorbance measurement.
## Signal and useful question

The output is dimensionless absorbance or optical density at a declared wavelength and path length. Candidate uses include tracking a reproducible optical change in a research assay or checking a preparation against a qualified reference range. Converting the reading into cell concentration requires a separate sample-specific relationship.
## Define the valid range

At high attenuation, stray light and detector limits can distort the response. At low attenuation, reference noise can dominate. A growth curve should therefore identify observations outside the qualified range rather than treating every recorded number as equally informative.

This candidate is most naturally associated with a defined liquid or optical-path assay. Its interpretation should not be imported into whole-plate imaging without evidence. The platform should preserve wavelength, path and preprocessing metadata so that researchers can distinguish biological trends from differences in optical configuration.
tables: Blank reference, optical path, detector linearity and response across the intended range.
Multiple scattering, coloured media, sedimentation, bubbles, path-length variation and stray light.
Stable source and detector geometry, reproducible vessel positioning and reference management.
Useful dynamic range and repeatability under the actual sample format.

pages.title: S18 Thermal infrared radiometry
text: **S18 · Environmental and research candidate · Surface radiometry**

Thermal infrared radiometry estimates temperature-related information from emitted radiation. The estimate depends on emissivity, reflected background radiation, optical transmission and the detector calibration. A thermal camera observes an accessible radiating surface; it does not automatically measure the temperature of material hidden beneath a lid.
## Signal and useful question

Raw signals are detector responses, while calibrated outputs may be radiance or apparent surface temperature in degrees Celsius or kelvin. Candidate questions include whether there are spatial thermal gradients, whether an assembly is heating unevenly or whether a process has departed from its qualified conditions.
## Do not confuse thermal structure with metabolic heat

A warmer region can result from lighting, airflow or electronics. Demonstrating a biological heat signal requires a much more controlled heat-flow measurement than observing apparent surface temperature. The instrument should not label a thermal image a biomass or susceptibility map without an independently validated relationship.

The proposed initial use is engineering characterization and environmental research. A thermal observation can help locate a fault or gradient, but its relationship to the plate’s relevant internal conditions must be tested. The uncertainty and emissivity assumptions should remain available to anyone interpreting the image.
tables: Traceable temperature reference, emissivity assumptions, optical path and spatial response.
Reflections, changing emissivity, vessel transmission, viewing angle and ambient background.
Appropriate infrared optics, unobstructed view and comparison with contact references.
Surface-temperature information that cannot be obtained adequately with simpler placed sensors.

pages.title: S19 Microcalorimetry
text: **S19 · Biological observation candidate · Heat-flow research**

Microcalorimetry measures small heat flows associated with physical, chemical or biological processes. In a controlled assay, changes in heat production can provide a time-resolved signal. The measured heat is the sum of relevant processes in the measurement volume and is not inherently specific to microbial growth.
## Signal and useful question

The primary output is thermal power, typically expressed in watts at an appropriate scale, and its time integral is energy in joules. Published work has investigated isothermal microcalorimetry for antimicrobial susceptibility research in defined sample contexts. [R45]
## Preserve the distinction from temperature sensing

A temperature sensor measures a local thermal state. A calorimeter estimates heat flow through a calibrated thermal relationship. Adding several temperature sensors does not automatically create a qualified calorimeter.

This candidate belongs to a dedicated research instrument or assay track. The first evaluation should establish baseline and response behaviour before asking a biological question. Any future susceptibility result would require a method-specific interpretation and comparison with a suitable reference. The cumulative heat curve should remain linked to its raw baseline, model assumptions and actual observation intervals, particularly when a run is interrupted.
tables: Electrical or other suitable heat reference, baseline stability and thermal response time.
Environmental drift, equilibration, chemical reactions, vessel differences and changing heat transfer.
Strong thermal control, sensitive differential measurement and a carefully defined sample interface.
A reproducible assay signal with acceptable detection time and baseline uncertainty.

pages.title: S20 Electrical impedance spectroscopy
text: **S20 · Biological observation candidate · Frequency-dependent electrical response**

Electrical impedance spectroscopy measures the relationship between an applied alternating signal and the resulting electrical response across frequency. Resistance, capacitance and interfacial effects can contribute to the complex impedance. In biological systems, the measured response may involve cells, medium, electrodes and geometry simultaneously.
## Signal and useful question

Outputs include impedance magnitude in ohms, phase in degrees or radians, and fitted model parameters. Published AST research has used several electrical measurement formats with different response mechanisms and timing constraints. Their results should be interpreted within those specific assays. [R38] [R40] [R41]
## Explain the fitted circuit

Equivalent-circuit parameters are model-based estimates. Different circuits may fit similar data, so a numerical fit should not be assigned a biological meaning without supporting evidence. Retain the measured spectrum, fitting range, residuals and parameter uncertainty.

This is a separate assay research pathway rather than an automatic add-on to endpoint plate reading. Evaluation should compare the electrical result with an appropriate reference and assess whether the relevant antimicrobial mechanism produces a measurable response within the proposed window. Short electrical acquisition time alone is not total time to a reportable result.
tables: Open, short and suitable reference loads; frequency response; electrode and geometry characterization.
Medium conductivity, temperature, electrode polarization, fouling, bubbles and contact variation.
Analog front end, controlled electrodes or microfluidics, shielding and electrical sample compatibility.
A stable signal linked to the intended response beyond medium and electrode changes.
